claim: Hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells in the adult mammalian bone marrow ensure blood cell renewal.
source: Hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells in the adult mammalian bone marrow ensure blood cell renewal.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mammalian hematopoiesis.

claim: The cellular microenvironment of hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells, called 'niche', regulates hematopoiesis both under homeostatic and immune stress conditions.
source: Their cellular microenvironment, called 'niche', regulates hematopoiesis both under homeostatic and immune stress conditions.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on the hematopoietic niche.

claim: In the Drosophila hematopoietic organ, the lymph gland, the posterior signaling center (PSC) acts as a niche to regulate the hematopoietic response to immune stress such as wasp parasitism.
source: In the Drosophila hematopoietic organ, the lymph gland, the posterior signaling center (PSC) acts as a niche to regulate the hematopoietic response to immune stress such as wasp parasitism.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The hematopoietic response to wasp parasitism relies on the differentiation of lamellocytes, a cryptic cell type, dedicated to pathogen encapsulation and killing.
source: This response relies on the differentiation of lamellocytes, a cryptic cell type, dedicated to pathogen encapsulation and killing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and established knowledge about Drosophila immune responses.

claim: Toll/NF-κB pathway activation in the PSC in response to wasp parasitism non-cell autonomously induces the lymph gland immune response.
source: Here, we establish that Toll/NF-κB pathway activation in the PSC in response to wasp parasitism non-cell autonomously induces the lymph gland immune response.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data including genetic manipulations and immunostaining.

claim: Co-activation of Toll/NF-κB and EGFR signaling by ROS levels in the PSC/niche controls lymph gland hematopoiesis under parasitism.
source: Our data further establish a regulatory network where co-activation of Toll/NF-κB and EGFR signaling by ROS levels in the PSC/niche controls lymph gland hematopoiesis under parasitism.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing ROS-dependent activation of both pathways.

claim: In adult mammals, Hematopoietic Stem and Progenitor Cells (HSPCs) present in the bone marrow are at the origin of blood cell production throughout an individual's life.
source: In adult mammals, Hematopoietic Stem and Progenitor Cells (HSPCs) present in the bone marrow are at the origin of blood cell production throughout an individual's life.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mammalian hematopoiesis.

claim: Self-renewal, proliferation and differentiation of HSPCs are under the control of the bone marrow microenvironment called the 'niche' which has emerged as a key regulator of hematopoiesis.
source: Self-renewal, proliferation and differentiation of HSPCs are under the control of the bone marrow microenvironment called the 'niche' which has emerged as a key regulator of hematopoiesis (Calvi and Link, 2015; Morrison and Scadden, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Processes that take place in the hematopoietic niche in response to infection and inflammation remain more elusive than those under normal conditions.
source: While considerable effort has been directed toward uncovering the mechanisms that regulate HSPC/niche communication under normal conditions, processes that take place in response to infection and inflammation remain more elusive (Kobayashi et al., 2016; Zhao and Baltimore, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations indicating gaps in current knowledge.

claim: Many transcriptional regulators and signaling pathways controlling blood cell development are conserved between insects and humans.
source: With the discovery that many transcriptional regulators and signaling pathways controlling blood cell development are conserved between insects and humans, Drosophila has become an important model to investigate hematopoiesis under normal conditions and in response to immune stress (Letourneau et al., 2016; Martinez-Agosto et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Drosophila has become an important model to investigate hematopoiesis under normal conditions and in response to immune stress.
source: With the discovery that many transcriptional regulators and signaling pathways controlling blood cell development are conserved between insects and humans, Drosophila has become an important model to investigate hematopoiesis under normal conditions and in response to immune stress (Letourneau et al., 2016; Martinez-Agosto et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Immune cells in Drosophila, called hemocytes, contribute to innate immune defense.
source: Immune cells in Drosophila, called hemocytes, contribute to innate immune defense (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Two phases of hematopoiesis occur in Drosophila.
source: Two phases of hematopoiesis occur in Drosophila (Gold and Brückner, 2015; Holz et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A first wave of immune cell production takes place during embryogenesis and generates two types of hemocytes, plasmatocytes and crystal cells.
source: A first wave of immune cell production takes place during embryogenesis and generates two types of hemocytes, plasmatocytes and crystal cells, which are involved in phagocytosis and melanisation/wound healing, respectively (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Plasmatocytes are involved in phagocytosis.
source: A first wave of immune cell production takes place during embryogenesis and generates two types of hemocytes, plasmatocytes and crystal cells, which are involved in phagocytosis and melanisation/wound healing, respectively (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Crystal cells are involved in melanisation/wound healing.
source: A first wave of immune cell production takes place during embryogenesis and generates two types of hemocytes, plasmatocytes and crystal cells, which are involved in phagocytosis and melanisation/wound healing, respectively (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Plasmatocytes and crystal cells increase in numbers at larval stages and either circulate in the hemolymph or aggregate into pockets under the epidermis (sessile hemocytes).
source: Both cell types increase in numbers at larval stages and either circulate in the hemolymph or aggregate into pockets under the epidermis (sessile hemocytes) (Makhijani et al., 2011; Márkus et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A second wave of de novo hematopoiesis takes place in a larval specialized hematopoietic organ, the lymph gland.
source: A second wave of de novo hematopoiesis takes place in a larval specialized hematopoietic organ, the lymph gland, a multi-lobed organ which develops along the anterior cardiac tube, the aorta region (Jung et al., 2005; Krzemien et al., 2010a; Lanot et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The lymph gland is a multi-lobed organ which develops along the anterior cardiac tube, the aorta region.
source: A second wave of de novo hematopoiesis takes place in a larval specialized hematopoietic organ, the lymph gland, a multi-lobed organ which develops along the anterior cardiac tube, the aorta region (Jung et al., 2005; Krzemien et al., 2010a; Lanot et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: During the third larval stage, the anterior lobes of the mature lymph gland are composed of a medullary zone (MZ) containing progenitors (prohemocytes), a cortical zone (CZ) composed of differentiating plasmatocytes and crystal cells, and the posterior signaling center (PSC).
source: During the third larval stage, the anterior lobes of the mature lymph gland are composed of a medullary zone (MZ) containing progenitors (prohemocytes), a cortical zone (CZ) composed of differentiating plasmatocytes and crystal cells, and the posterior signaling center (PSC) (Jung et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: During metamorphosis, lymph gland rupture releases all hemocytes into circulation.
source: During metamorphosis, lymph gland rupture releases all hemocytes into circulation (Grigorian et al., 2011; Lanot et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A third blood cell type, called lamellocyte, differentiates in emergency situations, such as wasp parasitism, from lymph gland progenitors and circulating/sessile hemocytes.
source: A third blood cell type, called lamellocyte, differentiates in emergency situations, such as wasp parasitism, from lymph gland progenitors and circulating/sessile hemocytes (Anderl et al., 2016; Crozatier et al., 2004; Honti et al., 2010; Lanot et al., 2001; Márkus et al., 2009; Stofanko et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Lamellocytes are specialized hemocytes which mediate the encapsulation and killing of pathogens too large to be phagocytosed.
source: Lamellocytes are specialized hemocytes which mediate the encapsulation and killing of pathogens too large to be phagocytosed.
evidence: This is established knowledge about lamellocyte function.

claim: Following wasp egg laying inside the Drosophila larva, the egg is recognized as a foreign body.
source: Following wasp egg laying inside the Drosophila larva, the egg is recognized as a foreign body.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the immune response to wasp parasitism.

claim: Wasp egg recognition leads to differentiation of lamellocytes at the expense of other immune cells.
source: This leads to differentiation of lamellocytes at the expense of other immune cells (Honti et al., 2010; Krzemień et al., 2007; Márkus et al., 2009; Stofanko et al., 2010), the premature dispersal of the lymph gland and the release of lamellocytes into the hemolymph (Crozatier et al., 2004; Sorrentino et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Wasp egg recognition leads to the premature dispersal of the lymph gland and the release of lamellocytes into the hemolymph.
source: This leads to differentiation of lamellocytes at the expense of other immune cells (Honti et al., 2010; Krzemień et al., 2007; Márkus et al., 2009; Stofanko et al., 2010), the premature dispersal of the lymph gland and the release of lamellocytes into the hemolymph (Crozatier et al., 2004; Sorrentino et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The PSC plays a major role to control the immune response to wasp parasitism.
source: The PSC plays a major role to control the immune response to wasp parasitism (Benmimoun et al., 2015; Crozatier et al., 2004; Krzemień et al., 2007; Oyallon et al., 2016; Sinenko et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In the absence of PSC, such as in collier (col/kn/ebf) mutants, or upon its genetic ablation, massive differentiation of lamellocytes fails to occur.
source: In the absence of PSC, such as in collier (col/kn/ebf) mutants, or upon its genetic ablation, massive differentiation of lamellocytes fails to occur.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies on the PSC.

claim: Wasp parasitism increases Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) levels in PSC cells.
source: It was recently established that wasp parasitism increases Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) levels in PSC cells, leading to the secretion of Spitz (Spi), one ligand of the Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) signaling pathway (Sinenko et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Increased ROS levels in PSC cells lead to the secretion of Spitz (Spi), one ligand of the Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) signaling pathway.
source: It was recently established that wasp parasitism increases Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) levels in PSC cells, leading to the secretion of Spitz (Spi), one ligand of the Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) signaling pathway (Sinenko et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Spitz released from PSC cells activates the EGFR pathway in circulating hemocytes, inducing them to differentiate into lamellocytes.
source: These authors proposed that Spi released from PSC cells activates the EGFR pathway in circulating hemocytes, inducing them to differentiate into lamellocytes.
evidence: This is a proposal from a cited study (Sinenko et al., 2011).

claim: The evolutionarily conserved Toll/NF-κB pathway regulates Drosophila hematopoiesis both under homeostatic and wasp parasitism conditions.
source: Several independent studies established that the evolutionarily conserved Toll/NF-κB pathway regulates Drosophila hematopoiesis both under homeostatic and wasp parasitism conditions (Gao et al., 2016; Gueguen et al., 2013; Matova and Anderson, 2006, 2010; Qiu et al., 1998; Schmid et al., 2014; Sorrentino et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: How Toll/NF-κB controls wasp egg encapsulation remains unknown.
source: However, how Toll/NF-κB controls wasp egg encapsulation remains unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The Toll/NF-κB pathway is activated in PSC cells in response to egg laying by Leptopilina boulardi wasps.
source: Here, we show that this pathway is activated in PSC cells in response to egg laying by Leptopilina boulardi wasps and non-cell autonomously controls lamellocyte differentiation in the lymph gland.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Toll/NF-κB pathway activation in PSC cells non-cell autonomously controls lamellocyte differentiation in the lymph gland.
source: Here, we show that this pathway is activated in PSC cells in response to egg laying by Leptopilina boulardi wasps and non-cell autonomously controls lamellocyte differentiation in the lymph gland.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Toll/NF-κB pathway activation in PSC cells leads to lymph gland disruption.
source: This, in turn, leads to lymph gland disruption and in fine to successful wasp egg encapsulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Lymph gland disruption leads to successful wasp egg encapsulation.
source: This, in turn, leads to lymph gland disruption and in fine to successful wasp egg encapsulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: A regulatory network linking ROS to Toll/NF-κB in the PSC and to EGFR/Erk signaling in lymph gland progenitors controls the lymph gland response to parasitism.
source: We establish that a regulatory network linking ROS to Toll/NF-κB in the PSC and to EGFR/Erk signaling in lymph gland progenitors controls the lymph gland response to parasitism and the success of wasp egg neutralization.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The regulatory network linking ROS to Toll/NF-κB in the PSC and to EGFR/Erk signaling in lymph gland progenitors controls the success of wasp egg neutralization.
source: We establish that a regulatory network linking ROS to Toll/NF-κB in the PSC and to EGFR/Erk signaling in lymph gland progenitors controls the lymph gland response to parasitism and the success of wasp egg neutralization.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: 30 hr post-wasp egg laying, 93% of wild-type larvae lymph glands are disrupted.
source: 30 hr post-wasp egg laying, 93% of wild-type (wt) larvae lymph glands are disrupted, that is, lymph gland cells are released into circulation (Figure 1A,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In pll2/pll7 mutants, 98% of the lymph glands remain intact 30 hr post-parasitism.
source: In contrast, in pll2/pll7 mutants, 98% of the lymph glands remain intact (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: More than half of lymph glands are intact in parasitized Dif1 mutant 30 hr post-parasitism, while the others start disrupting.
source: Likewise, more than half of lymph glands are intact in parasitized Dif1 mutant, while the others start disrupting, that is, only some cells at the periphery of the anterior lobes disperse (Figure 1D,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: 48 hr post-parasitism, Dif and pll mutant lymph glands have disrupted.
source: At a later time point, 48 hr post-parasitism, Dif and pll mutant lymph glands have disrupted (Figure 1H,I), similar to previously reported for Tl and tube mutants (Sorrentino et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and a citation to published literature.

claim: dl1 lymph glands disrupt as in control larvae 30 hr post-parasitism.
source: dl1 lymph glands, however, disrupt as in control larvae (Figure 1E,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Lymph gland dispersal is delayed 30 hr post-parasitism in Dif1/Df(2L)J4 larvae compared to +/Df(2L)J4 controls and dl1/Df(2L)J4 larvae.
source: Corroborating these findings, lymph gland dispersal is delayed 30 hr post-parasitism in Dif1/Df(2L)J4 larvae - Df(2L)J4 removes both Dl and Dif - compared to +/Df(2L)J4 controls and dl1/Df(2L)J4 larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Delayed lymph gland disruption is observed in Dif1 but not dl1 isogenic mutant larvae.
source: Delayed lymph gland disruption is also observed in Dif1 but not dl1 isogenic mutant larvae, further ruling out a genetic background effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Toll/NF-κB signaling is required for the proper timing of lymph gland dispersal in response to wasp infection.
source: Collectively, these data show that Toll/NF-κB signaling is required for the proper timing of lymph gland dispersal in response to wasp infection and that Dif is the only NF-κB factor involved.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Dif is the only NF-κB factor involved in the proper timing of lymph gland dispersal in response to wasp infection.
source: Collectively, these data show that Toll/NF-κB signaling is required for the proper timing of lymph gland dispersal in response to wasp infection and that Dif is the only NF-κB factor involved.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Lymph gland dispersal in response to wasp parasitism is associated with the loss of the basement membrane surrounding the organ.
source: Lymph gland dispersal in response to wasp parasitism is associated with the loss of the basement membrane surrounding the organ, allowing the release of lamellocytes into circulation (Sorrentino et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In parasitized Dif1 mutant lymph glands, a continuous ECM layer surrounds the anterior lobes 20 hr post parasitism.
source: In contrast to control larvae (Figure 1J,L), immunostaining of parasitized Dif1 mutant lymph glands for an extracellular matrix (ECM) protein, the heparan sulfate proteoglycan Perlecan/Trol (Terribly Reduced Optic Lobes) (Dragojlovic-Munther and Martinez-Agosto, 2013; Grigorian et al., 2013) indicates the presence of a continuous ECM layer surrounding the anterior lobes 20 hr post parasitism (Figure 1K,M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The delayed lymph gland dispersal observed in Dif1 mutant is associated with basement membrane persistence.
source: Thus, the delayed lymph gland dispersal observed in Dif1 mutant is associated with basement membrane persistence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on ECM staining.

claim: 20 hr post-parasitism, lamellocytes are detected in control larvae but none are found in Dif1 and pll2/pll7 mutants.
source: 20 hr post-parasitism, lamellocytes are detected in control larvae (Figure 1N), whereas none are found in Dif1 and pll2/pll7 mutants (Figure 1O,P).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: 30 hr post-parasitism, while most control lymph glands have already released lamellocytes into circulation, few lamellocytes are detected in Dif1 and pll2/pll7 mutant lymph glands.
source: 30 hr post-parasitism, while most control lymph glands have already released lamellocytes into circulation (Figure 1Q), few lamellocytes are detected in mutant lymph glands (Figure 1R–S).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Toll/NF-κB signaling is essential for the timely differentiation of lamellocytes in the lymph gland.
source: Altogether, these data show that Toll/NF-κB signaling, while not required for lamellocyte differentiation per se, is essential for the timely differentiation of lamellocytes in the lymph gland, breakdown of its basement membrane, and lamellocyte release into the hemolymph.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Toll/NF-κB signaling is essential for breakdown of the lymph gland basement membrane.
source: Altogether, these data show that Toll/NF-κB signaling, while not required for lamellocyte differentiation per se, is essential for the timely differentiation of lamellocytes in the lymph gland, breakdown of its basement membrane, and lamellocyte release into the hemolymph.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Toll/NF-κB signaling is essential for lamellocyte release into the hemolymph.
source: Altogether, these data show that Toll/NF-κB signaling, while not required for lamellocyte differentiation per se, is essential for the timely differentiation of lamellocytes in the lymph gland, breakdown of its basement membrane, and lamellocyte release into the hemolymph.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Toll/NF-κB signaling is not required for lamellocyte differentiation per se.
source: Altogether, these data show that Toll/NF-κB signaling, while not required for lamellocyte differentiation per se, is essential for the timely differentiation of lamellocytes in the lymph gland, breakdown of its basement membrane, and lamellocyte release into the hemolymph.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing delayed but eventual lamellocyte differentiation in mutants.

claim: Lamellocytes mediate wasp egg encapsulation, which is critical for host survival since it prevents hatching of wasp larvae.
source: Upon parasitism, lamellocytes mediate wasp egg encapsulation, which is critical for host survival since it prevents hatching of wasp larvae (Crozatier et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Wasp egg hatching reliably reflects the success of the immune response.
source: Wasp egg hatching, which reliably reflects the success of the immune response (Mortimer et al., 2013; Schmid et al., 2014; Vanha-Aho et al., 2015), is impaired in either Dif1 (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) or pll2/pll21 and Tlrv1/Tlr mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Sorrentino et al., 2004) but not in dl1 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that Dif-mediated activation of Toll/NF-κB pathway is required for wasp egg encapsulation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Wasp egg hatching is impaired in Dif1 mutants.
source: Wasp egg hatching, which reliably reflects the success of the immune response (Mortimer et al., 2013; Schmid et al., 2014; Vanha-Aho et al., 2015), is impaired in either Dif1 (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) or pll2/pll21 and Tlrv1/Tlr mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Sorrentino et al., 2004) but not in dl1 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that Dif-mediated activation of Toll/NF-κB pathway is required for wasp egg encapsulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Wasp egg hatching is impaired in pll2/pll21 and Tlrv1/Tlr mutants.
source: Wasp egg hatching, which reliably reflects the success of the immune response (Mortimer et al., 2013; Schmid et al., 2014; Vanha-Aho et al., 2015), is impaired in either Dif1 (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) or pll2/pll21 and Tlrv1/Tlr mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Sorrentino et al., 2004) but not in dl1 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that Dif-mediated activation of Toll/NF-κB pathway is required for wasp egg encapsulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and a citation.

claim: Wasp egg hatching is not impaired in dl1 mutants.
source: Wasp egg hatching, which reliably reflects the success of the immune response (Mortimer et al., 2013; Schmid et al., 2014; Vanha-Aho et al., 2015), is impaired in either Dif1 (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) or pll2/pll21 and Tlrv1/Tlr mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Sorrentino et al., 2004) but not in dl1 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that Dif-mediated activation of Toll/NF-κB pathway is required for wasp egg encapsulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dif-mediated activation of Toll/NF-κB pathway is required for wasp egg encapsulation.
source: Wasp egg hatching, which reliably reflects the success of the immune response (Mortimer et al., 2013; Schmid et al., 2014; Vanha-Aho et al., 2015), is impaired in either Dif1 (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) or pll2/pll21 and Tlrv1/Tlr mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Sorrentino et al., 2004) but not in dl1 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that Dif-mediated activation of Toll/NF-κB pathway is required for wasp egg encapsulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on wasp egg hatching in various mutants.

claim: Lymph gland-derived lamellocytes are essential for successful wasp egg encapsulation.
source: These data, together with the delay in lymph gland disruption observed in Dif and pll mutants (Figure 1), strongly suggest that lymph gland-derived lamellocytes are essential for successful wasp egg encapsulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on lymph gland disruption and wasp egg hatching.

claim: Before lymph gland disruption, less than 10% of circulating hemocytes are lamellocytes.
source: Before disruption, which occurs around 20 hr post-parasitism in control larvae and 30 hr post parasitism in Dif1 mutants, less than 10% of circulating hemocytes are lamellocytes (Figure 2D,F,G,I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A few lamellocytes differentiate from sessile/circulating hemocytes prior to lymph gland dispersion.
source: This indicates that a few lamellocytes differentiate from sessile/circulating hemocytes prior to lymph gland dispersion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on circulating lamellocytes before lymph gland disruption.

claim: Following lymph gland disruption, more than 50% of circulating hemocytes are lamellocytes in both control and Dif1 mutant larvae.
source: Following lymph gland disruption, however, more than 50% of circulating hemocytes are lamellocytes in both control and Dif1 mutant larvae (Figure 2E,F,H,I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Lymph gland disruption causes a rapid and major increase in the number of circulating lamellocytes.
source: We thus conclude that lymph gland disruption causes a rapid and major increase in the number of circulating lamellocytes and that this is delayed in Toll/NF-κB mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on circulating lamellocytes before and after lymph gland disruption.

claim: The increase in circulating lamellocytes following lymph gland disruption is delayed in Toll/NF-κB mutants.
source: We thus conclude that lymph gland disruption causes a rapid and major increase in the number of circulating lamellocytes and that this is delayed in Toll/NF-κB mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on circulating lamellocytes in mutants.

claim: A delay in both lymph gland disruption and in the increase numbers of circulating lamellocytes is observed in parasitized wild-type larvae raised at 18°C.
source: A delay in both lymph gland disruption (data not shown) and in the increase numbers of circulating lamellocytes, is observed in parasitized wild-type larvae raised at 18°C (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that the lymph gland response is temperature-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The lymph gland response to parasitism is temperature-dependent.
source: A delay in both lymph gland disruption (data not shown) and in the increase numbers of circulating lamellocytes, is observed in parasitized wild-type larvae raised at 18°C (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that the lymph gland response is temperature-dependent.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on temperature effects.

claim: The dominant-negative JAK/STAT receptor latran (lat) down-regulates JAK/STAT signaling in lymph gland progenitors following wasp attack, allowing massive differentiation of lymph gland lamellocytes.
source: We had previously established that the dominant-negative JAK/STAT receptor latran (lat) (Eye transformer [Kallio et al., 2010]), down-regulates JAK/STAT signaling in lymph gland progenitors following wasp attack, allowing massive differentiation of lymph gland lamellocytes (Makki et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature from the authors' previous work.

claim: Knocking-down lat specifically in lymph gland progenitors impairs lymph gland dispersal post-parasitism.
source: Accordingly, we found that knocking-down lat specifically in lymph gland progenitors using double-stranded RNA-mediated interference (RNAi) (dome-MESO > lat RNAi) impairs lymph gland dispersal post-parasitism (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: 90% of wasp eggs hatched when lat was inactivated in progenitor cells compared to 10% in controls.
source: Moreover, 90% of wasp eggs hatched when lat was inactivated in progenitor cells (dome-MESO > lat RNAi) compared to 10% in controls (dome-MESO>), whereas no defect was observed when lat was inactivated in PSC cells (antp > lat RNAi) (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: No defect in wasp egg hatching was observed when lat was inactivated in PSC cells.
source: Moreover, 90% of wasp eggs hatched when lat was inactivated in progenitor cells (dome-MESO > lat RNAi) compared to 10% in controls (dome-MESO>), whereas no defect was observed when lat was inactivated in PSC cells (antp > lat RNAi) (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Lymph gland disruption and lamellocyte release into circulation are linked to successful wasp egg encapsulation.
source: Altogether, these data link lymph gland disruption and lamellocyte release into circulation to successful wasp egg encapsulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on lat knockdown effects.

claim: Dif is expressed in PSC cells.
source: Immunostaining of wt lymph glands shows that Dif is expressed in PSC cells (Figure 3A–A'') (Gueguen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and a citation.

claim: 6 hr post-parasitism, Dif is expressed in hematopoietic progenitors.
source: 6 hr post-parasitism, it is also expressed in hematopoietic progenitors (Figure 3B–B'').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: D4–lacZ is expressed in PSC cells in uninfected wt larvae.
source: In agreement with published data, D4–lacZ is expressed in PSC cells in uninfected wt larvae and upregulated in these cells 6 hr post parasitism, in addition to being expressed de novo in lymph gland progenitors (Figure 3C–C'', D–D'', E) (Gueguen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and a citation.

claim: D4–lacZ is upregulated in PSC cells 6 hr post parasitism.
source: In agreement with published data, D4–lacZ is expressed in PSC cells in uninfected wt larvae and upregulated in these cells 6 hr post parasitism, in addition to being expressed de novo in lymph gland progenitors (Figure 3C–C'', D–D'', E) (Gueguen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and a citation.

claim: D4–lacZ is expressed de novo in lymph gland progenitors 6 hr post parasitism.

claim: In pll2/pll7 mutants, D4-LacZ expression is still observed in the PSC under normal conditions.

claim: D4-LacZ is not expressed in the PSC in Dif1 mutants under normal conditions.

claim: Toll/NF-κB signaling is induced both in the PSC and in lymph gland progenitors in response to parasitism.

claim: Dif is the major NF-κB transactivator involved in Toll/NF-κB signaling in response to parasitism.

claim: Lymph gland disruption is dependent on lamellocyte differentiation.

claim: Toll/NF-κB signaling is required in PSC cells and not in lymph gland progenitors for the correct timing of lymph gland lamellocyte differentiation.

source: Altogether, these data show that Toll/NF-κB signaling is required in PSC cells and not in lymph gland progenitors for the correct timing of lymph gland lamellocyte differentiation, which leads to lymph gland dispersal and thus a successful cellular immune response against wasp parasitism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on tissue-specific knockdowns and wasp egg hatching.

claim: Parasitism induces a global oxidative stress in the lymph gland.
source: 6 hr post-parasitism, gstD-lacZ expression is increased in both the PSC (Figure 6B,C) (Sinenko et al., 2011) and the progenitors (Figure 6B,D), indicating that parasitism induces a global oxidative stress in the lymph gland.

claim: PSC downregulation of Duox or Nox did not prevent gstD-lacZ upregulation in PSC cells.

claim: Following parasitism, ROS are intrinsically produced by PSC cells, which in turn leads to oxidative stress in lymph gland progenitors.

A partial rescue of lymph gland dispersal was observed (Figure 6L).

claim: In response to wasp egg laying, ROS level increase in PSC cells leads to Toll/NF-κB activation and lymph gland dispersal.

claim: Decreasing ROS levels either in the PSC or in progenitors delays lymph gland lamellocyte differentiation.
source: Since 6 hr post parasitism gstD-lacZ is expressed in all lymph gland cells, we examined in which cells modifying ROS levels could affect the immune response. Decreasing ROS levels either in the PSC (col > catalase) or in progenitors (dome > catalase) delay lymph gland lamellocyte differentiation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), postpone lymph gland rupture (Figure 6L,M; Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–C) and enhance wasp egg hatching (Figure 6N,O).

claim: Decreasing ROS levels either in the PSC or in progenitors postpones lymph gland rupture.

Decreasing ROS levels either in the PSC (col > catalase) or in progenitors (dome > catalase) delay lymph gland lamellocyte differentiation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), postpone lymph gland rupture (Figure 6L,M; Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–C) and enhance wasp egg hatching (Figure 6N,O).

evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Increased ROS levels in both PSC cells and progenitors following parasitism are essential for the mounting of an efficient lymph gland response and for wasp egg encapsulation.
source: Thus, increased ROS levels in both PSC cells and progenitors following parasitism are essential for the mounting of an efficient lymph gland response and for wasp egg encapsulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on ROS manipulation in different cell types.

source: The incomplete rescue of lymph gland dispersal when simultaneously scavenging ROS and activating Toll/NF-κB signaling in PSC cells, suggested that additional signaling pathway(s) act downstream of ROS.

claim: p-ERK was detected in lymph gland progenitors 6 hr post parasitism, indicating EGFR activation.

source: In this process, the TLR (Toll-like Receptors)/NF-κB pathway is activated via TLR4 in mouse bone marrow endothelial cells, a component of the vascular niche (Boettcher et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The cellular immune response to parasitism in Drosophila can be compared to an emergency hematopoiesis.
source: The cellular immune response to parasitism in Drosophila can be compared to an emergency hematopoiesis.
evidence: This is a comparison drawn by the authors based on the characteristics of the response.

claim: The role of the EGFR pathway in mammalian hematopoiesis is largely unknown.
source: The role of the EGFR pathway in mammalian hematopoiesis is largely unknown (Kerpedjieva et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation indicating a gap in knowledge.

claim: Drosophila lamellocytes have been reported to differentiate both from sessile/circulating hemocytes of embryonic origin, and from larval lymph gland progenitors.
source: Drosophila lamellocytes have been reported to differentiate both from sessile/circulating hemocytes of embryonic origin, and from larval lymph gland progenitors (Anderl et al., 2016; Crozatier et al., 2004; Honti et al., 2010; Lanot et al., 2001; Márkus et al., 2009; Sorrentino et al., 2002; Stofanko et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: While few lamellocytes are found in circulation before lymph gland disruption, after disruption, their number sharply increases, constituting nearly half of all circulating hemocytes.
source: We found that, while few lamellocytes are found in circulation before lymph gland disruption, after disruption, their number sharply increases, constituting nearly half of all circulating hemocytes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on circulating hemocyte counts.

claim: Delaying lymph gland disruption impairs the success of wasp egg encapsulation.
source: We further observed that delaying lymph gland disruption impairs the success of wasp egg encapsulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on wasp egg hatching in mutants with delayed lymph gland disruption.

claim: The release of lymph gland lamellocytes is paramount for successful wasp egg neutralisation.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that the release of lymph gland lamellocytes is paramount for successful wasp egg neutralisation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on lamellocyte numbers and wasp egg encapsulation success.

claim: Wasp parasitism activates Toll/NF-κB in the lymph gland.
source: We have shown here that wasp parasitism activates Toll/NF-κB in the lymph gland.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Drosomycin-GFP expression was not observed in response to wasp parasitism in the lymph gland.
source: Drosomycin-GFP expression was, however, not observed in response to wasp parasitism in the lymph gland (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F), in agreement with previous observations that antimicrobial peptides are not produced in larvae under these conditions (Nicolas et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and a citation.

claim: Antimicrobial peptides are not produced in larvae under wasp parasitism conditions.

evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Dif target genes activated in the lymph gland under parasitism are specific to this response.
source: This suggests that Dif target genes activated in the lymph gland under parasitism are specific to this response.

claim: Constitutive activation of Toll/NF-κB in PSC cells impairs the permeability barrier of the PSC.
source: A recent study established that constitutive activation of Toll/NF-κB in PSC cells impairs the permeability barrier of the PSC, possibly facilitating diffusion of signal(s) from the PSC to lymph gland progenitors (Khadilkar et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Oxidative stress, in particular reactive oxygen species (ROS), regulates hematopoiesis both in mammals and in Drosophila.
source: Oxidative stress, in particular reactive oxygen species (ROS), regulates hematopoiesis both in mammals and in Drosophila (Ludin et al., 2014; Owusu-Ansah and Banerjee, 2009; Sinenko et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In mammals, there is a complex interplay between ROS and NF-κB signaling during hematopoiesis.
source: In mammals, there is a complex interplay between ROS and NF-κB signaling during this process.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian hematopoiesis.

claim: Oxidative stress can either affect IκB kinase complex (IKK) activity in the cytoplasm or NF-κB DNA-binding capacity in the nucleus.
source: Oxidative stress can either affect IκB kinase complex (IKK) activity in the cytoplasm or NF-κB DNA-binding capacity in the nucleus (Gupta et al., 2014; Siomek, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In the fly lymph gland, increased ROS levels are observed in both the PSC and hematopoietic progenitors in response to parasitism.
source: In the fly lymph gland, increased ROS levels are observed in both the PSC and hematopoietic progenitors in response to parasitism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on gstD-lacZ expression.

claim: ROS increase in lymph gland progenitors could reflect changes in cell metabolism since progenitors actively divide as an immediate response to parasitism.
source: ROS increase in lymph gland progenitors, which could reflect changes in cell metabolism since progenitors actively divide as an immediate response to parasitism (Krzemien et al., 2010b; Sorrentino et al., 2002), is dependent on ROS production by PSC cells.
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to published literature on progenitor proliferation.

claim: ROS increase in lymph gland progenitors is dependent on ROS production by PSC cells.
source: ROS increase in lymph gland progenitors, which could reflect changes in cell metabolism since progenitors actively divide as an immediate response to parasitism (Krzemien et al., 2010b; Sorrentino et al., 2002), is dependent on ROS production by PSC cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that ROS scavenging in PSC cells reduces ROS in progenitors.

claim: ROS-induced signaling in both PSC cells and progenitors is required to trigger wasp-induced dispersal of the lymph gland and release of lamellocytes into circulation.
source: ROS-induced signaling in both PSC cells and progenitors is required to trigger wasp-induced dispersal of the lymph gland and release of lamellocytes into circulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on ROS manipulation in different cell types.

claim: ROS-dependent Toll/NF-κB activation following infection by the Wolbachia bacteria was reported in the mosquito Aedes aegypti.
source: ROS-dependent Toll/NF-κB activation, following infection by the Wolbachia bacteria, was reported in the mosquito Aedes aegypti, but the mechanism involved was not defined (Pan et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.
